Matrix Protein 1 (M1) Conservation:

Out of 253 codons, 192 sites (75.9%) were identified under strong pervasive purifying selection with a posterior probability \(\ge 0.90\).
This extreme conservation explains why the regional designs (Indo-only and SEA-only) were able to place highly sensitive primers in the forward block (codons 63 to 117, corresponding to nucleotide positions 187–352 bp).

Matrix Protein 2 (M2) Conservation:

Out of 98 codons, only 25 sites (25.5%) were identified under purifying selection. M2 exhibits higher sequence entropy than M1, particularly in its extracellular domain (ectodomain), making it less suitable for diagnostic design.

title: Results: Selection Pressure & Site Conservation
text:
2. Episodic Diversifying Selection (MEME Analysis)
MEME was run to detect transient, branch-specific evolutionary events that standard site-level models miss:

Identified Episodic Sites in M1:

Only 2 codons (Codons 30 and 235) exhibited evidence of episodic positive selection with a p-value \(\le 0.05\).
Diagnostic Veto: Codon 30 is located upstream of the primary forward primer target (which starts at nucleotide position 187). The Bridge Scoring Engine (Module 07) successfully detected this selection marker and applied a spatial penalty, ensuring that primer annealing coordinates remain downstream of codon 30.

Identified Episodic Sites in M2:

6 codons (Codons 11, 13, 18, 36, 59, and 93) exhibited episodic selection. The clustering of these positive selection sites in the M2 segment highlights the risks of placing diagnostic primers in this gene region.

title: Results: Selection Pressure & Site Conservation
section: 3. M1 vs. M2 Selection Pressure Divergence
text:
3. M1 vs. M2 Selection Pressure Divergence
The stark contrast in selection pressure between the two matrix proteins highlights their differing biological constraints:

Structural Constraint (M1): The M1 protein is a structural matrix shell that must interact closely with the viral envelope, the ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, and the cytoplasmic tail of the M2 protein. This complex web of physical interactions severely constrains the protein’s sequence space, meaning almost any amino acid change impairs viral assembly and budding. This translates to the 75.9% pervasive purifying selection rate observed, consistent with the high sequence conservation of the M1 gene documented in global surveillance data (Bhatt et al. 2011).
Immune & Drug Selection (M2): The M2 protein is a proton-selective ion channel essential for viral uncoating (Pinto and Lamb 2006). Its extracellular ectodomain is exposed to host antibodies, driving immune escape selection pressure. Simultaneously, its transmembrane pore domain is under strong drug-mediated selection from adamantane antivirals (amantadine and rimantadine), which directly drove the global fixation of the S31N substitution in the pore region (Hayden 2006; Deyde et al. 2007). Consequently, the purifying selection rate drops to 25.5%, reflecting the high evolutionary plasticity of this gene and rendering it an unreliable target for long-term diagnostic assay stability.

title: Results: Selection Pressure & Site Conservation
section: 4. Bridge Scoring Profile & Physical Target Selection
text:
4. Bridge Scoring Profile & Physical Target Selection
The Bridge Scoring Engine (Module 07) integrated site-specific conservation (Shannon Entropy) with HyPhy FUBAR purifying selection probabilities using a weighted core scoring formula:
\[\text{Core Score} = 0.66 \times (1 - \text{Entropy}) + 0.34 \times \text{Prob(dN < dS)}\]
This core score was computed across the entire segment. Because the engine was configured with the full_segment strategy for the Influenza A MP segment, it evaluated the segment from 0 to 1027 bp as a single candidate region (segment-MP_region_1). The resulting overall scores and grades for this target region are:

Indonesia Only: Core composite score of 0.4071 (Grade D, mean entropy: 0.2146, conservation: 89.27%).
Southeast Asia Only: Core composite score of 0.4098 (Grade D, mean entropy: 0.2025, conservation: 89.87%).
All-Partial Database: Core composite score of 0.4022 (Grade D, mean entropy: 0.2359, conservation: 88.20%).


Downstream Primer Coordinate Selection (Module 08 & 09)
Although Module 07 exported the entire segment as a single candidate zone (due to the segment’s small size and overall conservation), the downstream primer design tool (Primer3/PrimerLab in Module 08 and 09) scanned this candidate region to select the most stable physical primer coordinates, demonstrating how local sequence variations alter target selection:

Indonesia Only Design: The optimal primers were placed in the M1 gene at 187–341 bp (Forward primer: 187–218 bp, Reverse primer: 310–341 bp), generating a 155 bp amplicon.
Southeast Asia Only Design: The primers were placed at 187–352 bp (Forward: 187–216 bp, Reverse: 321–352 bp), generating a 166 bp amplicon.
All-Partial Database Design: When global database variations were introduced, increased sequence entropy in the M1 gene (including at codon 30) forced the primer design tool to shift coordinates to the 3’ end of the segment in the M2 gene at 858–1008 bp (Forward: 858–889 bp, Reverse: 978–1008 bp), generating a 151 bp amplicon.

title: Module 09: BLAST Specificity Verification
text: Even thermodynamically optimal primers can fail in clinical settings if they cross-react with host genomes or non-target pathogens. Module 09 executes the NCBI BLAST+ Specificity Verification Engine (scripts/m09_blast_verification.py) to screen all PrimerLab candidates, filtering out primer sets that risk generating off-target amplification.

1.1. Local Mode (mode: local)

Databases: Queries custom local database structures built upstream by build_db.smk:

human_db: A consolidated human reference database combining the GRCh38.p14 and T2T-CHM13v2.0 assemblies.
virus_db: A database containing common non-target respiratory pathogens (e.g., Adenovirus, Rhinovirus, Enterovirus, RSV, SARS-CoV-2) to ensure no cross-reactivity.

Advantage: High-throughput execution (10–100x faster than remote queries), completely secure (clinical target sequences are not uploaded to public servers), and runs offline.



1.2. Remote Mode (mode: remote)

Database: Queries the massive NCBI nt (nucleotide) database remotely via the Web BLAST API.
Advantage: Queries the most up-to-date sequence library globally, capturing newly deposited viral strains.
Requirement: Highly recommended to set the NCBI_API_KEY environment variable; otherwise, public NCBI rate limits will trigger frequent connection drops and search timeouts.

title: Module 09: BLAST Specificity Verification
section: 2. The 3’ End Veto Filter and Penalty Scoring
text:
2. The 3’ End Veto Filter and Penalty Scoring
The specificity engine does not rely on simple identity percentages. Instead, it evaluates the biochemical risk of off-target priming:

3’ End Critical Zone: The 3’ terminal region of a primer is the site of active DNA polymerase extension. A mismatch at the 5’ end of a primer is tolerated, but a mismatch in the last 5 to 8 nucleotides of the 3’ end will block amplification.
The Veto Rule: If the 3’ critical zone of both the forward and reverse primers binds to the same off-target template (such as a human chromosome) with zero mismatches, and within a PCR-amplify-capable distance (\(\le 1000\text{ bp}\)), the candidate set is immediately vetoed (FAIL).
Blast Penalty Calculation: Candidates with minor, non-critical off-target hits (e.g., single-primer bindings or matches with multiple 3’ mismatches) are not excluded but receive a weighted penalty score. This penalty is integrated into the final selection rank: \[\text{Specificity Score} = 100 - \sum \text{Off-target Penalties}\]

6. Troubleshooting & Limitations

6.1. Remote BLAST Execution Hangs or Returns Gateway Timeouts

Problem: When running in remote mode, the Snakemake pipeline hangs for hours or terminates with 504 Gateway Timeout or HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.
Cause: This is caused by high traffic on NCBI public servers, combined with a lack of a validated user API Key. NCBI limits unauthenticated remote requests to 3 per second, which is quickly exceeded when checking 100 candidates.
Solution: Register a free account at NCBI to obtain an API key, then export the environment variable NCBI_API_KEY in your shell before starting the run:
export NCBI_API_KEY=your_ncbi_api_key_string
Alternatively, configure mode: local and build local BLAST databases to bypass NCBI rate limits completely.

text: To track how pathogens evolve across transmission pathways, the pipeline must identify mutational events at every node in the phylogenetic tree. Module 06 performs Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction (ASR) at both the nucleotide and amino acid levels, and exports the integrated phylogenetic dataset for interactive visualization in Auspice.

title: Module 06: Mutational Annotation
text:
1. Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction (ASR)
ASR determines the most likely genetic sequence of extinct viral ancestors at the internal nodes of the phylogenetic tree. This allows the pipeline to map exactly where and when specific mutations arose along the branches:

Nucleotide ASR (augur ancestral): Evaluates the nucleotide states at each node using a joint maximum-likelihood inference algorithm implemented in TreeTime (Sagulenko et al. 2018). It outputs a JSON file (nt_muts.json) mapping nucleotide mutations relative to the parent nodes (e.g. G120A indicating a Guanine to Adenine change at position 120).
Amino Acid Translation & Mutation Calling (augur translate): Translates nucleotide sequences into amino acids for all coding genes (CDS) defined in the GFF3 annotation file. It automatically handles splicing and codon reading frames, outputting a JSON file (aa_muts.json) detailing non-synonymous mutations (e.g., M1: I109T representing an Isoleucine to Threonine substitution at codon 109 of the M1 protein).

title: Module 06: Mutational Annotation
text:

Nucleotide and amino acid mutations mapped to every node and tip.

text:
6. Troubleshooting & Limitations

6.1. Invalid Codon Length Warnings

Problem: augur translate throws multiple warnings: Codon length is not a multiple of 3 or Skipping translation for gene X.
Cause: Gaps inserted in the middle of sequences during multiple sequence alignment can disrupt the open reading frame. If a codon is truncated (e.g. only 2 nucleotides remain), translation fails.
Solution: Ensure that the upstream alignment phase (Module 03) is anchored tightly using a high-quality reference and --fill-gaps parameter, and that coding sequence regions are extracted precisely according to GFF coordinates in Module 05.

title: Module 04: Phylodynamic Reconstruction
text: Reconstructing the evolutionary history and transmission timelines of viral lineages is critical for tracking pathogen dissemination. Module 04 executes a phylodynamic workflow: inferring a Maximum-Likelihood (ML) phylogenetic tree, followed by refinement into a calendar-dated “timetree” to model mutational rates over time.

title: Module 04: Phylodynamic Reconstruction
text:
1. Maximum-Likelihood Tree Inference (IQ-TREE 2)
The raw tree inference is performed by the Snakemake rule augur_tree which invokes the IQ-TREE 2 engine (Minh et al. 2020) via the augur tree wrapper (Hadfield et al. 2018).
  ┌────────────────────────────────┐
  │         aligned.fasta          │
  └───────────────┬────────────────┘
                  │
                  ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │         augur tree         │
  ├────────────────────────────┤
  │   Infer raw ML phylogeny   │
  │   --method iqtree          │
  └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │        tree_raw.nwk        │
  └────────────────────────────┘

Substitution Model: By default, IQ-TREE automatically selects the best-fit nucleotide substitution model (typically GTR+I+G or similar) based on the alignment’s base frequencies and mutational patterns.
Optimization: Multi-threading is enabled (configured via augur.threads in config.yaml) to distribute likelihood evaluation steps across multiple cores, accelerating tree searches for large datasets.

title: Module 04: Phylodynamic Reconstruction
text:
2. Temporal Refinement (TreeTime)
The raw ML tree represents distances in terms of substitutions per nucleotide site. To convert these distances into calendar dates, the Snakemake rule augur_refine utilizes the TreeTime algorithm (Sagulenko et al. 2018) via the augur refine wrapper.
┌─────────────────┐      ┌───────────────┐      ┌─────────────────┐
│  tree_raw.nwk   ├─────►│  aligned.fasta├─────►│  metadata.tsv   │
└────────┬────────┘      └───────┬───────┘      └────────┬────────┘
         │                       │                       │
         └───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘
                                 ▼
                    ┌──────────────────────────┐
                    │       augur refine       │
                    ├──────────────────────────┤
                    │ Max-Likelihood Timetree  │
                    │ --clock-rate 0.003       │
                    │ --stochastic-resolve     │
                    └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                 │
                   ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                   ▼                           ▼
      ┌─────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐
      │        tree.nwk         │ │   branch_lengths.json   │
      │   (Dated Newick Tree)   │ │   (Substitution Rates)  │
      └─────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘
The refinement process applies the following computational controls:

Molecular Clock Modeling: Fits a strict molecular clock (with a default rate of \(0.003\) substitutions/site/year and a standard deviation of \(0.0015\) for Influenza A) using metadata collection dates.
Stochastic Polyotomy Resolution: Resolves multi-forking nodes (polytomies) using a stochastic likelihood approach to produce a binary tree structure, preventing artificial branch clustering.
Rooting: Finds the optimal root of the tree that maximizes the temporal correlation (root-to-tip regression) between sequence divergence and collection dates.

3.1. Parameter Tuning Dictionary









Parameter Name
Allowed Values
Default Value
Purpose & Biological Meaning




phylodynamics.clock_rate
Float \(\ge 0.0\)
0.003
The baseline mutation velocity (substitutions per site per year). For Influenza A MP, the slow rate of \(1.87 \times 10^{-3}\) fits within this prior distribution. If designing for a hyper-variable virus like HIV or SARS-CoV-2, this should be increased (e.g. 0.006 or 0.008).

3.2. How to Interpret Molecular Clock Fitting
Module 04 refines the branch lengths into real calendar years:

Root-to-Tip Distance: The slope of the regression line of root-to-tip genetic distance versus time represents the estimated evolutionary rate. If the data points deviate heavily from the regression line, it indicates a poor fit (high sequencing errors or mislabeled collection dates).
Clock-dated Nodes: Reviewing the nodes in the calendar tree allows validating the evolutionary history (e.g., ensuring the separation of major clades matches historical pandemic records, such as the 2009 H1N1 emergence).

title: Module 04: Phylodynamic Reconstruction
text:
5. Troubleshooting & Limitations

5.1. Tree Refinement Failure (Outliers)

Problem: augur refine terminates with an error pointing to “large clock deviations” or “negative branch lengths”.
Cause: Sequences with wrong collection dates (e.g. historical samples mislabeled with modern dates) act as extreme phylogenetic outliers, breaking the root-to-tip regression.
Solution: Review the execution logs in logs/{build}/m04_augur_refine.log to identify the outlier sequence names. These outliers can be placed in an exclusion list (exclude.txt) and filtered out during the Stage 2 subsampling phase.

title: Module 02: Quality Control & Subsampling
text:
Raw viral sequencing data from global databases contains significant sampling biases, sequence duplicates, and low-quality assemblies. Module 02 resolves these issues by implementing a two-stage quality control and spatio-temporal subsampling pipeline before phylogenetic reconstruction.
The module ensures phylogenetic trees and genetic selection analyses are computed on a high-quality, representative, and computationally tractable subset of genomes.

title: Module 02: Quality Control & Subsampling
text:
1. Stage 1: Quality Control & Prefiltering
The first stage runs the Snakemake rule qc_prefilter which executes scripts/qc_prefilter.py using BioPython (Cock et al. 2009). It applies three main filters:

N-Content Filtering: Sequences with high rates of ambiguous bases (\(N\)) are discarded. Ambiguous bases prevent accurate alignment and mutation identification. The threshold is set via config["qc"]["max_n_content"] (default: 5.0%).
Sequence Deduplication: Replicating sequences with identical nucleotide structures are identified via MD5 hashing and collapsed. This deduplication reduces downstream alignment and tree-building times by up to 60% without losing unique mutational variants.
Underrepresented Subtype Filtering: Subtypes with fewer than a minimum count (default: 30 sequences) are filtered out to ensure statistical validity during genetic selection analysis.

title: Module 02: Quality Control & Subsampling
text:
2. Stage 2: Spatio-Temporal Subsampling (Augur Filter)
To prevent phylogenetic trees from being dominated by regions with massive sequencing capacity (creating a sampling bias), the Snakemake rule augur_filter runs scripts/m02_filter_wrapper.py. This wrapper dynamically executes augur filter (Hadfield et al. 2018) using a Focal + Contextual Subsampling strategy.
                    ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                    │  Prefiltered Sequences FASTA │
                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   │
                   ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
                   ▼                               ▼
      ┌─────────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────────┐
      │   Focal Subsampling     │     │ Contextual Subsampling  │
      ├─────────────────────────┤     ├─────────────────────────┤
      │ Targets domestic area   │     │ Targets global partners │
      │ High sequence density   │     │ Representative samples  │
      │ e.g. Country: Indonesia │     │ e.g. MY, SG, AU, CN, IN │
      └────────────┬────────────┘     └────────────┬────────────┘
                   │                               │
                   └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                                   ▼
                      ┌─────────────────────────┐
                      │    Combine & Deduplicate│
                      ├─────────────────────────┤
                      │ filtered_sequences.fasta│
                      └─────────────────────────┘

2.1. Focal Sampling

Target: The domestic region under investigation (configured via subsampling.focal.query). For this build, it selects Indonesian isolates (country == 'Indonesia').
Density: Retains a high density of local sequences to capture the complete picture of local transmission chains.



2.2. Contextual Sampling

Target: The neighboring travel corridors identified in our BPS demographic justification (Malaysia, Singapore, Australia, China, India, Japan).
Density: Subsamples global sequences at a lower density (e.g., grouped by country, year, and month) to serve as evolutionary context for ancestral reconstruction.

text:
5. Troubleshooting & Limitations

5.1. Ambiguous Date Exclusions

Problem: Crucial local sequences are missing in the final alignment.
Cause: Augur filter defaults to dropping sequences with incomplete dates (e.g. 2024-XX-XX or 2024-06-XX). If the command includes --exclude-ambiguous-dates-by any, these are excluded.
Solution: The pipeline’s metadata sanitizer (Module 01) resolves this by dynamically filling day or month wildcards with standard middle-points (e.g. 15 for day, 06 for month) when exact temporal precision is not mandatory for downstream selection analyses.

title: Scientific Literature
text: This section provides the scientific rationale, mathematical formulations, and literature background supporting the methodology used in our target discovery pipeline.

title: Scientific Literature
section: 1. Molecular Diagnostics: Beyond Static Shannon Entropy
text:
1. Molecular Diagnostics: Beyond Static Shannon Entropy
Traditional molecular diagnostic design relies almost exclusively on sequence conservation metrics calculated from contemporary isolates, most notably Shannon Entropy (Equation 1).
\[H(x) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i) \log_2 P(x_i)\]
Where \(P(x_i)\) is the probability of observing nucleotide or amino acid \(x_i\) at alignment position \(x\).

The Limitations of Shannon Entropy
While Shannon Entropy is effective at measuring static sequence conservation, it suffers from critical limitations:

Temporal Blindness: Entropy only captures variation at a single snapshot in time. It cannot distinguish between a position that is temporarily conserved due to sampling bias or recent clonal expansion, and one that is conserved due to strict functional constraints.
Lack of Functional Context: It treats all mutations equally, failing to capture the biological fitness costs associated with specific nucleotide substitutions (Capra and Singh 2007). For instance, a conservative mutation (maintaining residue properties) is weighted identically to a disruptive one.



Diagnostic Escape and Primer Mismatches
In clinical diagnostics, relying on static conservation frequently leads to diagnostic escape or signature erosion. Studies on SARS-CoV-2 PCR assays demonstrated that circulating genomic mutations rapidly accumulate at primer and probe binding sites, significantly reducing binding affinity and leading to false-negative clinical results (Khan et al. 2020).
Crucially, mutations located at the 3’ terminus of the primers have the most detrimental effect on PCR amplification, as they directly impede the extension activity of DNA polymerases (Vanaerschot et al. 2020). This makes structural and selection-aware design a vital tool to future-proof diagnostic targets.


The Evolutionary-Aware Paradigm
To overcome these limitations, our pipeline integrates evolutionary dynamics:

Purifying Selection Detection: By mapping codon-by-codon evolutionary selection pressures, we identify target sites under strict purifying selection (\(dN/dS \ll 1\)). Mutations at these sites are functionally deleterious to the pathogen, meaning any mutant strain is rapidly eliminated by natural selection.
Ancestral Sequence Reconstruction (ASR): By reconstructing the historical ancestral states at internal nodes of the phylogenetic tree, we trace the evolutionary inertia of genomic regions. Target regions with high ancestral-to-contemporary conservation (high Bridge Score) represent genomic zones that have remained locked across evolutionary time, making them highly resilient to future mutations.

title: Scientific Literature
text:
2. Research Design & Workflow Framework
Designing a pipeline capable of processing thousands of viral genomes with strict reproducibility requires a robust framework. Below is the scientific justification for our software architecture choices:

2.1. Snakemake: Workflow Orchestration & Reproducibility
For enterprise-grade diagnostic target discovery, script-based pipelines are insufficient. We utilize Snakemake (Mölder et al. 2021) as our workflow management system.

Deterministic Dependency Resolution: Snakemake isolates each execution module (M01-M10) into distinct conda environments, preventing package version mismatch.
Traceability and Log Auditing: Every step records CLI inputs, environment parameters, and logs, ensuring the pipeline meets clinical validation standards.



2.2. Nextstrain: Spatio-Temporal Genomic Surveillance
For tracking pathogen lineages globally, we utilize the Nextstrain architecture (Hadfield et al. 2018).

Clade and Lineage Definition: Nextstrain provides real-time tracking of emerging variants, allowing us to select representative datasets.
Phylogeographic Subsampling: To avoid geographic bias, we subsample sequences relative to case numbers and demographic travel data (informed by BPS data), preventing overrepresented sequences from skewing conservation scores.

title: Scientific Literature
text:
3. Core Bioinformatics Algorithms

3.1. Alignment: MAFFT (Multiple Sequence Alignment)
Aligning thousands of viral genomes requires high speed without sacrificing alignment quality at the codon level.

Algorithm: We use MAFFT (Katoh and Standley 2013), applying the progressive method FFT-NS-2 for large datasets and iterative refinement (L-INS-i) for sub-datasets. MAFFT’s fast Fourier transform approximation allows rapid alignment of highly variable regions while preserving structural codon boundaries.



3.2. Phylogeny and ASR: IQ-TREE 2
Phylodynamic tree reconstruction and ancestral sequence states are computed using IQ-TREE 2 (Minh et al. 2020).

Substitution Model Selection: IQ-TREE 2 integrates ModelFinder to automatically select the optimal nucleotide or codon substitution model (e.g., GTR+I+G4) based on Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC).
Ancestral Reconstruction: IQ-TREE 2 utilizes Empirical Bayes maximum likelihood methods to perform marginal and joint ancestral sequence reconstruction at all phylogenetic nodes, providing the raw inputs for our Bridge Scoring engine.



3.3. Selection Pressure: HyPhy (Hypothesis Testing using Phylogenies)
To calculate site-specific selection pressures, we use HyPhy (Pond et al. 2020).

FUBAR (Fast Unconstrained Bayesian Approximation): FUBAR (Murrell et al. 2013) employs a fast Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to calculate the posterior probability of purifying selection (\(dN < dS\)) at each codon site. FUBAR is selected for its high processing speed on large alignments.
MEME (Mixed Effects Model of Episodic Selection): MEME (Murrell et al. 2012) is used to detect codons experiencing transient, episodic positive selection along a fraction of branches, ensuring we filter out target regions susceptible to localized adaptation.

title: Scientific Literature
text:
4. Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RAA/RPA) Design
Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) and its close derivative, Recombinase Amplification Assay (RAA), operate isothermally (typically at 37–42°C) (Piepenburg et al. 2006).

Diagnostic Oligonucleotide Requirements
RAA chemistry demands distinct target parameters compared to conventional PCR:

Primer Length: RAA primers are significantly longer (30–35 bp) than PCR primers (18–22 bp).
Probe Length: RAA probes (typically Exo probes) require a length of 46–52 bp with internal fluorophores and quencher modifications.
Thermodynamic Mismatch Tolerance: Because RAA operates isothermally, longer primers exhibit a substantial tolerance to template mismatches, successfully amplifying sequences even with multiple mismatches (up to 9 mismatches across primer/probe binding sites) (Daher et al. 2016). However, mismatches located at the 3’ terminus of RAA primers still significantly reduce amplification kinetics, requiring the target site to be located on extremely conserved regions to maintain maximum sensitivity. We calculate these parameters using nearest-neighbor thermodynamic models to exclude stable secondary structures.

section: 3. How to Interpret & Validate Reference Alignments
text:
3. How to Interpret & Validate Reference Alignments
The reference genome acts as the “anchor” for the entire pipeline. During Module 03 (Alignment), the raw sequences are mapped against the reference:

Coordinate Drift: If the selected reference sequence is too divergent from the target population (e.g. using a 1934 H1N1 reference for a 2026 seasonal design), the alignment will suffer from excessive gaps. This will cause coordinate mismatch downstream.
CDS Mapping: Ensure the references.annotation matches the reference sequence exactly. If the coordinates in the GFF file do not match the exons in the FASTA reference, the translation step in Module 05 (Selection Pressure) will fail, producing frame-shift errors or early stop codons in the HyPhy input.







ImportantVerification Step



Before initiating a run, verify that the reference FASTA header matches the GFF sequence ID exactly (e.g. both must read NC_002016.1). If they do not match, Snakemake will crash in Module 03 due to reference header mismatch.

3. Epidemiological Risk Profiles
Each country represents a distinct epidemiological corridor, justifying why our diagnostic target discovery pipeline must account for their circulating viral sequences:

3.1. Malaysia & Singapore: Direct Border Corridors
Due to physical proximity and high-frequency business travel, Malaysia and Singapore represent the most immediate pathways for introduction. Emerging variants in Southeast Asia typically transition through these commuter corridors within days of global detection.


3.2. Australia: Southern Hemisphere Seasonal Shift
Influenza and respiratory virus transmission in the Southern Hemisphere is temporally shifted by approximately 6 months compared to the Northern Hemisphere. Monitoring sequences from Australia allows our pipeline to capture mutations that arise during the Southern Hemisphere winter season, future-proofing diagnostic assays ahead of the next Indonesian seasonal wave.


3.3. China & Japan: East Asian Evolutionary Epicenter
Historically, many dominant Influenza lineages (especially avian and seasonal strains) originate in East Asian transmission hubs. China’s high-density agricultural-urban interfaces and Japan’s massive transit hubs serve as evolutionary hot spots where novel mutations first stabilize before propagating globally.


3.4. India: South Asian Regional Transit Hub
India is a major population center and travel gateway in South Asia. Its high density and complex demographic corridors facilitate rapid viral evolution and reassortment. Including Indian sequences ensures that South Asian lineage transitions are well-represented in the background dataset, preventing assay failure for imported lineages originating from the subcontinent.

title: Home
text:
Executive Summary
Pathogens with epidemic potential, particularly those causing Acute Respiratory Infections (ARI) such as Influenza A and Coronaviruses, exhibit high mutation rates. Conventional molecular diagnostics (e.g., RT-PCR and Recombinase Polymerase Amplification - RAA) frequently suffer from diagnostic escape due to primer mismatch at target sites.
To address this challenge, our pipeline integrates global genomic surveillance data with phylogenetic and evolutionary selection pressure analyses. By mapping codon-by-codon evolutionary dynamics, the pipeline identifies target regions under strong purifying selection (negative selection) and high ancestral conservation. Targeting these genetically constrained regions ensures the longevity and diagnostic sensitivity of designed assays, mitigating the risk of diagnostic escape.

title: Module 01: Data Acquisition
text:
This module serves as the primary entry point for the pandemic preparedness diagnostic pipeline. Its main objective is to retrieve raw viral nucleotide sequences (FASTA) and associated spatio-temporal metadata (TSV) from global public health repositories (NCBI GenBank or GISAID) or handle manual local datasets.
The module ensures that raw inputs are cleaned, standardized, and enriched with initial clade/lineage classifications before downstream processing.

1.1. Path A: Automated NCBI Datasets API
When configured with database: ncbi, the pipeline utilizes the official NCBI Datasets CLI tool (Sayers et al. 2022) to programmatically fetch data.

Sequence Download: The pipeline downloads the genomic datasets as a compressed zip package:
datasets download virus genome taxon "Influenza A virus" \
    --geo-location "Asia/Indonesia" \
    --include genome \
    --filename results/influenza-a-mp-universal/m01/ncbi_dataset.zip
Unzipping & Data Extraction: The genome sequences are extracted, and the structural data report is converted into tabular format using dataformat:
dataformat tsv virus-genome \
    --inputfile ncbi_dataset/data/data_report.jsonl \
    --fields accession,virus-name,geo-location,geo-region,collection-date,release-date,length,host-name \
    > results/influenza-a-mp-universal/m01/raw_metadata.jsonl
Column Mapping: The extracted tabular fields are mapped to Nextstrain Augur compatible naming conventions:

Accession \(\rightarrow\) strain
Virus Name \(\rightarrow\) virus
Geographic Location \(\rightarrow\) location
Geographic Region \(\rightarrow\) region
Collection Date \(\rightarrow\) date
Release Date \(\rightarrow\) date_submitted
Length \(\rightarrow\) length
Host Name \(\rightarrow\) host




1.2. Path B: Local / Manual Files (GISAID EpiFlu & Manual Portals)
When configured with database: local, the pipeline processes manually downloaded files, such as metadata sheets from GISAID (Shu and McCauley 2017).

Sequence Copy: Copies the raw FASTA file from the path specified in config["local_input"]["sequences"] to the pipeline directory.
Format-Aware Metadata Conversion:

NCBI Virus Web CSV: If format is ncbi_virus_csv, it maps columns and splits the combined Geo_Location (e.g., Indonesia: Java: Jakarta) into country (Indonesia) and region (Java).
TSV / GISAID: If format is gisaid_epiflu or gisaid_tsv, columns are copied as-is and forwarded to the downstream sanitizer.

title: Module 01: Data Acquisition
text:
2. Metadata Sanitization & 3-Tier Column Validation
Different databases output metadata with varying schemas, date formats, and missing entries. The Snakemake rule sanitize_metadata runs scripts/sanitize_metadata.py to normalize the tabular data into a consistent internal format using a 3-tier validation protocol:

Tier 1: Critical (strain, date, country)

Action: Must be present and valid. Any rows with empty strain IDs or completely unparseable dates (e.g., missing year) are dropped from the analysis to prevent pipeline failure.
Incomplete Dates: Imprecise dates like 2024 or 2024-05 are normalized to 2024-XX-XX or 2024-05-XX to comply with Nextstrain’s date format requirements.

Tier 2: Spatio-Temporal Context (region, host, division)

Action: Missing values are silently filled with defaults. If host is empty, it defaults to Human. If region is missing, it is derived from country mapping.

Tier 3: Metadata Pass-through

Action: Non-essential demographic fields (e.g., age, gender, passage_history) are passed through unmodified to maintain dataset richness.

title: Module 01: Data Acquisition
text:
3. Nextclade Clade & Lineage Classification
If Nextclade is enabled (nextclade.enabled: true in config), the raw sequences are aligned and classified using the Nextclade CLI tool (Aksamentov et al. 2021):

Dataset Retrieval: Fetches the specified Nextclade reference database (e.g., nextstrain/flu/h1n1pdm/ha/MW626062 for Influenza H1N1 HA):
nextclade dataset get --name "nextstrain/flu/h1n1pdm/ha/MW626062" --output-zip nextclade_dataset.zip
Nextclade Alignment & QC Run: Runs sequence alignment, mutation calling, clade classification, and frameshift detection:
nextclade run \
    --input-dataset nextclade_dataset.zip \
    --output-tsv nextclade.tsv \
    early_filtered_sequences.fasta
Metadata Enrichment: The rule enrich_metadata merges the base metadata table with the Nextclade output table (nextclade.tsv) using accession IDs, appending critical columns such as clade, subclade, and quality control scores (qc.overallStatus).

5.1. NCBI API Rate Limiting (HTTP 429)

Problem: Running the NCBI API pathway frequently fails with HTTP Error 429: Too Many Requests.
Cause: NCBI limits unauthenticated requests to 3 per second.
Solution: Obtain an NCBI API Key from your NCBI account page and export it to your shell environment prior to executing the pipeline:

This raises the rate limit to 10 requests per second.



5.2. Missing Package Dependencies in Nextclade

Problem: Nextclade CLI command is not found or fails to execute.
Solution: Ensure the Snakemake rule is running in the correct Conda environment (envs/nextstrain.yaml). If executing manually, nextclade can be installed via:
conda install -c conda-forge nextclade

title: Module 03: Multiple Sequence Alignment
text: Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) is a foundational step in viral phylogenomics. Module 03 aligns the filtered, high-quality query sequences against a standardized reference genome to establish a unified coordinate system for mutation calling, selection pressure profiling, and diagnostic target design.

title: Module 03: Multiple Sequence Alignment
text:
1. Multiple Alignment Methodology
The module executes the Snakemake rule augur_align which wraps the MAFFT alignment engine (Katoh and Standley 2013) through Nextstrain’s Augur Toolkit (Hadfield et al. 2018).
┌────────────────────────────────┐
│   filtered_sequences.fasta     │
└───────────────┬────────────────┘
                │
                ├────────────────◄ Reference: NC_002016.1
                ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │         augur align        │
  ├────────────────────────────┤
  │   Align against reference  │
  │   --fill-gaps              │
  │   --remove-reference       │
  └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
┌────────────────────────────────┐
│         aligned.fasta          │
└────────────────────────────────┘
The alignment workflow applies the following computational procedures:

Reference-Based Coordinate Stabilization: Rather than performing a de novo alignment (which can shift coordinates if insertion mutations are present), queries are aligned relative to the reference sequence (NC_002016.1 for Influenza A MP). This ensures that every position in the output alignment corresponds exactly to the official NCBI reference coordinates.
Gap Filling (--fill-gaps): Deletions or missing sequences at the \(5'\) and \(3'\) ends are automatically padded with ambiguous bases (\(N\)) instead of alignment gaps (\(-\)). This padding prevents downstream tools (especially HyPhy selection pressure scripts) from misinterpreting missing terminal sequencing data as evolutionary deletion events.
Thread Optimization: Scaling the alignment is achieved by partitioning input query streams across multiple CPU cores (configured via augur.threads in config.yaml), allowing rapid alignment of thousands of sequences.

Crucial Diagnostic Veto. Forces MAFFT to keep the exact length of the reference sequence. Any insertions in the query sequences that extend beyond the reference length are discarded (clipped), and deletions are padded with gaps (\(-\)). 2.2. How to Interpret Alignment Visualizations
During alignment, sequences are padded at the terminal ends:

Terminal N Padding: If a query sequence begins at nucleotide 5 (e.g., due to primer clipping during wet-lab sequencing), the alignment will pad positions 1–4 with NNNN. This is expected and does not count as a true mutation.
Internal Gaps (-): A gap represents a deletion mutation. If a gap occurs in a target primer region, it represents a major mismatch that will block recombinase or polymerase binding.

title: Module 03: Multiple Sequence Alignment
text:
4. Troubleshooting & Limitations

4.1. Terminal Insertion Loops (Gaps)

Problem: Downstream translation of alignment (augur translate) fails with “invalid codon length” or indicates massive frameshifts.
Cause: Heavy insertion mutations in non-standard isolates can introduce gaps (\(-\)) in the middle of sequences that break the 3-nucleotide codon reading frame.
Solution: Switch from standard MAFFT parameters to codon-aware alignment (e.g. using MACSE) if the target virus is highly divergent. For Influenza A segment 7, MAFFT combined with reference anchoring is highly stable and does not suffer from frame disruptions.

title: Module 05: Selection Pressure Engine
text:
Evolutionary pressure shapes pathogen genomes, driving the emergence of diagnostic escape mutations. Module 05 calculates codon-specific selection pressures (\(dN/dS\) ratios) using the HyPhy (Hypothesis Testing using Phylogenies) software suite (Pond et al. 2020).
By identifying sites under purifying (negative) selection, the pipeline targets positions that are evolutionarily stable, ensuring long-term diagnostic assay durability.

title: Module 05: Selection Pressure Engine
text:
1. Diversity-Aware Subsampling & Reading Frame Extraction
Because molecular evolutionary selection models scale non-linearly with sequence counts, the pipeline partitions sequence data before selection profiling:

Diversity-Aware Subsampling (scripts/hyphy_subsample.py): Subsamples the global MSA into a representative subset (default: 50 to 2000 sequences) using a balanced stratification strategy based on subtype x country x year metadata. This maintains evolutionary diversity while reducing the computational load from thousands to a few hundred sequences.
Coding-Gene Extraction (scripts/extract_genes.py): Slices the nucleotide sequence alignments into distinct open reading frames (ORFs) based on the CDS coordinate annotations in the input GFF3 file (e.g., extracting \(M1\) and \(M2\) genes for the Influenza A MP segment).
Harsh Masking: Codons containing frame-breaking insertions, deletions, or high rates of ambiguous bases (\(N\)) are masked out. This step is critical because codon selection analyses require gap-free, in-frame codon triplets (length divisible by 3) to execute.
Phylogenetic Tree Pruning (scripts/prune_tree.py): Prunes the main dated tree (tree.nwk) to only retain the tips present in the subsampled gene alignment, preventing tree-alignment dimension mismatches.

title: Module 05: Selection Pressure Engine
text:
2. Selection Pressure Profiling Models
The engine executes two complementary selection models to discover mutations:

2.1. Pervasive Selection Analysis (FUBAR)
Pervasive (constant) selection pressure across the entire phylogeny is calculated using the FUBAR (Fast Unconstrained Bayesian Approximation) model (Murrell et al. 2013):

Objective: Computes the posterior probability of non-synonymous (\(dN\)) and synonymous (\(dS\)) substitution rates per codon site.
Purifying Selection: Codon positions with \(dN/dS < 1\) (specifically \(dN < dS\) with a posterior probability threshold \(\ge 0.9\)) are classified as conserved sites under negative selection. These sites are the primary targets for diagnostic primer and probe design.



2.2. Episodic Selection Analysis (MEME)
Periodical or branch-specific selection pressure is modeled using the MEME (Mixed Effects Model of Episodic Selection) model (Murrell et al. 2012):

Objective: Detects individual codon sites subject to episodic diversifying selection (positive selection occurring on only a subset of lineages/branches).
Relevance: Identifies hotspots where transient mutations arise (e.g., vaccine escape or antiviral resistance sites), which must be flagged as high-risk regions to avoid in diagnostic design.

HyPhy’s FUBAR and MEME computations scale non-linearly with sequence count. Setting a limit of 300 sequences balances statistical accuracy and execution speed (averaging ~10 minutes per run). Increasing this beyond 1000 can lead to days of computation on standard CPUs.

The minimum sample size. Below 50 sequences, the statistical power of FUBAR is insufficient to resolve site-by-site selection patterns safely.

The significance level (p-value). Codons with a MEME p-value \(\le 0.05\) are flagged as undergoing episodic positive selection (mutational hot-spots).

Module 05 outputs raw JSON files (fubar_M1.json and meme_M1.json):

FUBAR Columns: Look for the parameters alpha (synonymous rate, \(dS\)) and beta (non-synonymous rate, \(dN\)). If beta is close to 0 and prob_negative is high (\(\ge 0.90\)), this site is extremely stable and a gold-standard target for diagnostic design.
MEME Columns: Look for p-value. A low value indicates that at least one branch of the phylogenetic tree has experienced sudden diversification. These coordinates must be avoided.

title: Module 05: Selection Pressure Engine
text:
5. Troubleshooting & Limitations

5.1. HyPhy Stale Cache Dimension Mismatches

Problem: HyPhy exits with a fatal error: Index out of range or Matrix dimensions do not match.
Cause: When running FUBAR or MEME, HyPhy automatically generates and reads a binary cache file (e.g. *.FUBAR.cache) in the input folder. If you rerun the pipeline with a different number of sequences, the old cache size will conflict with the new alignment.
Solution: The Snakemake pipeline resolves this by programmatically purging any existing *.cache files in the output directory before invoking HyPhy.

title: Module 07: Bridge Scoring Engine
text:
Designing highly sensitive molecular diagnostic assays (such as PCR or RPA) requires identifying target regions that are both highly conserved in current strains and evolutionarily stable against future escape mutations.
Module 07 implements the Bridge Scoring Engine (scripts/m07_bridge_builder.py). The engine resolves a fundamental biological challenge: integrating whole-genome conservation data (nucleotide level) with codon-specific natural selection models (protein level) into a single, unified coordinate system.

title: Module 07: Bridge Scoring Engine
text:
1. The Dual-Track Integration Challenge
To understand the Bridge Engine, we must examine why data is split into whole-genome and gene-sliced tracks upstream:
                  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                  │          aligned.fasta (M03)            │
                  └────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────┘
                               │                      │
       [TRACK A: Whole-Sequence Track]      [TRACK B: Sliced-Gene Track]
                               │                      │
                (No slicing - processed as whole)     (Sliced by CDS GFF3 coordinates)
                               │                      │
                               ▼                      ▼
                  ┌─────────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │  Shannon Entropy Scan   │   │ Selection Pressure Scan  │
                  │  (Nucleotide level,     │   │ (Codon level, HyPhy      │
                  │   sites 1 to 1027)      │   │  FUBAR/MEME per gene)    │
                  └────────────┬────────────┘   └─────────────┬────────────┘
                               │                              │
                               └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                                              ▼
                                 ┌──────────────────────────┐
                                 │      Bridge Engine       │
                                 │   (Coordinate Remap &    │
                                 │    Biomechanical Scoring)│
                                 └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                              ▼
                                 ┌──────────────────────────┐
                                 │ conserved_regions.bed    │
                                 │ primer_targets_manifest  │
                                 └──────────────────────────┘

1.1. Track A: Whole-Sequence Nucleotide Scan (Shannon Entropy)

Why Whole Sequence? PCR primers and diagnostic probes can physically bind to any region along the viral segment—including non-coding regions (5’ UTR and 3’ UTR) which are often highly conserved. Therefore, nucleotide conservation (Shannon Entropy) must be calculated continuously across the entire alignment without skipping any positions.
Calculation: For each nucleotide column \(i\) in the alignment (positions 1 to 1027 for Influenza A MP), Shannon Entropy (\(H_i\)) is calculated based on base frequencies: \[H_i = - \sum_{b \in \{A, T, G, C, -\}} P(b) \log_2 P(b)\] A score of \(0.0\) indicates absolute conservation (100% of sequences share the same base).



1.2. Track B: Sliced-Gene Codon Scan (dN/dS Selection Pressure)

Why Sliced Genes? Natural selection pressures—synonymous (\(dS\)) and non-synonymous (\(dN\)) substitution rates—are defined by amino acid translations. Non-coding regions (UTRs) do not contain codons and cannot be analyzed by selection models. Thus, alignments must be sliced into individual coding sequences (CDS) (e.g., \(M1\) and \(M2\) genes) to run HyPhy FUBAR/MEME.

title: Module 07: Bridge Scoring Engine
text:
2. Coordinate Remapping & Score Fusion
The Bridge Engine merges these two tracks by mapping the codon-level selection scores from HyPhy back onto the exact nucleotide positions of the whole-sequence reference genome using coordinate boundaries extracted from the GFF3 annotation file.

2.1. Remapping Logic
For a coding gene \(G\) starting at nucleotide position \(Start_G\) in the whole genome:

Each codon position \(C\) (1-indexed) in the HyPhy output corresponds to three nucleotide positions in the whole sequence: \[\text{Nucleotide positions} = \{ Start_G + 3(C - 1), \;\; Start_G + 3(C - 1) + 1, \;\; Start_G + 3(C - 1) + 2 \}\]
Example (Influenza A M1 Gene): The \(M1\) gene starts at nucleotide position 26 on the MP segment. If HyPhy FUBAR identifies codon 10 as being under strong purifying selection, the Bridge Engine remaps this score to nucleotide positions 53, 54, and 55 on the whole sequence (\(26 + 3(10 - 1) = 53\)).



2.2. Handling Non-Coding Regions (UTRs)
Because UTRs lack codon structures and selection data, the Bridge Engine assigns them a neutral selection penalty (recombination/selection penalty = \(0\)). These regions are scored solely on their nucleotide Shannon Entropy and local mutation frequencies.

title: Module 07: Bridge Scoring Engine
section: 3. Targeting Strategies: Windowed vs. Full Segment
text:
3. Targeting Strategies: Windowed vs. Full Segment
Depending on the length and layout of the viral genome, the Bridge Engine can be configured to run in one of two distinct strategies:

3.1. Sliced Window Strategy (strategy: windowed)

How it works: The engine scans the alignment using a sliding window of a fixed size (e.g., 150 bp). Each window is scored individually.
Use Case: Ideal for long genomes (like SARS-CoV-2, ~30,000 bp). It breaks the genome into small target zones, allowing the pipeline to select and rank only the highest-scoring zones (S or A+) for downstream primer design.



3.2. Full Segment Strategy (strategy: full_segment)

How it works: The engine does not slice the sequence. Instead, it treats the entire viral segment (e.g., all 1027 bp of the Influenza A MP segment) as a single, contiguous target candidate.
Use Case: Ideal for short viral segments (such as Influenza MP or HA, ~1000 bp) where the segment is short enough to be passed directly to the primer design tool.
Impact on Grading: In this mode, the entire segment receives one overall composite score and grade (often a lower grade like C or D if the segment contains variable regions). The local “zone grading” becomes irrelevant because we are not picking subset windows; rather, we are exporting the entire IUPAC consensus sequence to let PrimerLab scan and design primers across the whole segment.

title: Module 07: Bridge Scoring Engine
text:
4. Biomechanical Scoring & Grading System
To evaluate target regions, the engine implements a multi-parametric Core \(\times\) Multipliers scoring function.

4.1. Core Score Calculation
The base core score is calculated by weighting normalized nucleotide conservation (\(Cons_{norm}\)) and FUBAR codon purifying selection probability (\(FUBAR_{prob}\)):

Normalized Conservation: Shannon Entropy (\(H\)) is normalized to a \([0, 1]\) scale: \[Cons_{norm} = 1.0 - \frac{\text{Mean Entropy}}{2.0}\]
Coding regions (CDS): \[\text{Core Score} = (w_{cons} \times Cons_{norm}) + (w_{fub} \times FUBAR_{prob})\] (Default weights: \(w_{cons} = 0.66\) and \(w_{fub} = 0.34\))
Non-coding regions (UTRs): \[\text{Core Score} = Cons_{norm} \times 0.95\]



4.2. Biomechanical Multipliers (Penalties)
The Core Score is multiplied by penalty multipliers (values \(\le 1.0\)) to discount regions with undesirable thermodynamic or mechanical traits: \[\text{Final Score} = \text{Core Score} \times M_{MEME} \times M_{recomb} \times M_{GC} \times M_{block} \times M_{homo}\]

Episodic Selection (\(M_{MEME}\)): Penalizes regions with sites undergoing transient positive selection (episodic escape hotspots).
Recombination (\(M_{recomb}\)): Multiplies by \(0.5\) if the region is close to recombination breakpoints.
GC-Content (\(M_{GC}\)): Lowers the score if the GC content falls outside the thermodynamically optimal range (\(40\% - 60\%\)).
Conserved Block (\(M_{block}\)): Penalizes windows lacking long contiguous conserved blocks.
Homopolymer (\(M_{homo}\)): Applies a penalty if the sequence contains homopolymer repeats (e.g., \(\ge 5\) identical nucleotides).



4.3. Target Grade Classification
The calculated Final Score determines the target grade and recommendation:








Grade
Final Score Range
Recommendation & Description




S
\(\ge 0.95\)
Optimal Target — Highest conservation, no selection danger; gold standard for universal primers.


A+
\(\ge 0.90\)
High-Priority Target — Near-optimal conservation with negligible evolutionary risk.


A
\(\ge 0.85\)
Recommended Target — Strong conservation profile with minor penalties.


A-
\(\ge 0.80\)
Acceptable Target — Suitable for validation, minor biomechanical caveats.


B+
\(\ge 0.75\)
Moderate Priority — Satisfactory conservation with moderate penalties.


B
\(\ge 0.70\)
Low Priority — Requires careful thermodynamic validation.


C
\(\ge 0.60\)
At-Risk Target — Significant penalties; not recommended without review.


D
\(< 0.60\)
Excluded — Failed critical biomechanical or evolutionary constraints.

title: Module 07: Bridge Scoring Engine
text:
5. Configuration & Parameterization
The Bridge Scoring Engine is configured in config.yaml to define search strategies and weights for evolutionary conservation versus selection pressure:
# [M07] Bridge scoring and window definitions
bridge:
  strategy: "full_segment"        # Treat whole segment as target (options: sliding_window, full_segment)
  design_regions:
    - "segment-MP"
  include_utr: true
  min_region_length: 150
  scoring:
    core:
      conservation_weight: 0.66   # Weight for Shannon Entropy conservation score (0.0 to 1.0)
      purifying_weight: 0.34      # Weight for HyPhy FUBAR negative selection probability (0.0 to 1.0)

5.1. Parameter Tuning Dictionary









Parameter Name

"sliding_window", "full_segment"

Defines how target regions are carved. "sliding_window" divides the genome into slices, which is ideal for long genomes (like Coronaviruses). "full_segment" passes the entire segment, which is ideal for short segments (like Influenza MP) so PrimerLab can scan the whole region.

The weight given to HyPhy FUBAR purifying selection probability. A high weight favors codons that are evolutionary forbidden to mutate, ensuring the diagnostic target will remain stable against future drift.





5.2. How to Interpret Target Grades
Module 07 outputs a targets list (primer_targets_manifest.yaml):

Grade S / A+: Highly recommended for design. Indicates a conserved hot-spot under strong negative selection.
Grade D: If running in full_segment mode, a Grade D is normal and represents the average variability of the entire segment. It should not be used as a veto; PrimerLab will still perform localized scans to find optimal candidate positions.

text:
7. Troubleshooting & Limitations

7.1. Low Scores in Full Segment Mode

Problem: In full_segment mode, the composite score is very low (e.g. \(0.40\)), resulting in Grade D.
Cause: Evaluating an entire 1000+ bp segment as a single window includes hyper-variable loops and non-coding mutations, accumulating homopolymer and mismatch penalties that lower the score.
Solution: This is expected behavior. The grade in full_segment mode is not used to exclude the segment, but simply reflects overall segment variation. The consensus sequence is still successfully exported to PrimerLab, which will perform local thermodynamic sliding scans to find individual primer pairs.

title: Module 08: Primer & Probe RAA Design
text:
Isothermal amplification technologies, such as Recombinase Aid Amplification (RAA) and Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA), are vital for point-of-care (POC) molecular diagnostics. Unlike thermal cycling PCR, RAA operates at a constant low temperature (\(37^\circ\text{C}\) to \(42^\circ\text{C}\)).
Module 08 integrates PrimerLab-Genomic, an in-house tool developed by the CORE-Lab Research group (GitHub Repository). PrimerLab-Genomic utilizes the core engine of Primer3 (Koressaar and Remm 2007; Untergasser et al. 2012) for candidate search and incorporates the ViennaRNA (Lorenz et al. 2011) package to evaluate complex secondary structures under isothermal, high-magnesium conditions.

title: Module 08: Primer & Probe RAA Design
section: 1. Biophysical and Thermodynamic Rules for RAA Design
text:
1. Biophysical and Thermodynamic Rules for RAA Design
RAA reaction dynamics differ fundamentally from traditional PCR. Because the double-stranded DNA template is unwound by a recombinase-primer complex rather than heat denaturation, the primers must satisfy strict biophysical criteria:
                       ◄─── 30 to 35 bp Forward Primer ───►
5'- ... NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN ... -3'
        ||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||
3'- ... NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN ... -5'
                                            ▲
                     [Critical 3' End: 100% Conserved (No IUPAC)]

1.1. Primer and Probe Dimensions

Primer Length: RAA primers must be 30 to 35 nucleotides long (compared to 18–22 bp for PCR). Shorter primers cannot form a stable recombinase filament and fail to initiate strand exchange at \(37^\circ\text{C}\).
Amplicon Length: The ideal product size range is 100 to 300 base pairs (maximum 500 bp) to ensure rapid amplification within 15–20 minutes under isothermal conditions.
Exo-Probe Structure: Fluorescent RAA exo-probes must be 46 to 52 nucleotides long. The probe sequence is modified internally:

An abasic site analog, Tetrahydrofuran (THF / dSpacer), is placed in the middle (at least 30 bp from the 5’ end and 15 bp from the 3’ end).
A Fluorophore (e.g., FAM) and a Quencher (e.g., BHQ-1) are attached immediately adjacent to the THF site.
A 3’ blocking group (e.g., phosphate or C3 spacer) prevents the probe from acting as a primer. During hybridization, the enzyme Exonuclease III cleaves the THF site, separating the fluorophore from the quencher to generate a fluorescent signal.




1.2. Temperature & Salt Corrections
Isothermal assay dynamics require distinct salt formulations (typically \(14\text{ mM}\) Magnesium acetate \([Mg^{2+}]\) and \(50\text{ mM}\) monovalent cations \([K^+]\)).
To ensure accurate melting temperature (\(T_m\)) prediction, PrimerLab-Genomic integrates thermodynamic parameters with salt-correction corrections (Lorenz et al. 2011) adjusted to these high-magnesium conditions. Standard PCR formulas underestimate the stabilizing effect of \(14\text{ mM}\) \(Mg^{2+}\), which raises the effective \(T_m\) of long primers.

title: Module 08: Primer & Probe RAA Design
text:
2. Evolutionary Exclusion Check
To prevent diagnostic escape (false negatives caused by ongoing viral evolution), the Snakemake rule m08_generate_payload programmatically extracts high-entropy positions and positive selection sites (identified by MEME/ASR in Modules 05 & 06) and converts them into Exclusion Blocks:

3’ End Protection: Primers are strictly forbidden from having any mutations or degenerate bases within the last 5 to 8 nucleotides of their 3’ end. Mismatches at the 3’ terminal block prevent DNA polymerase extension, causing assay failure.
Probe Body Protection: Probes are restricted from containing high-entropy coordinates to maintain binding stability.

title: Module 08: Primer & Probe RAA Design
text:
3. Degenerate Rescue System
In highly variable viral genomes, finding a 100% conserved 30–35 bp target is frequently impossible. Module 08 resolves this through the Degenerate Rescue Engine (scripts/m08_degenerate_rescue.py):

IUPAC Incorporation: If a position within a candidate primer has a Minor Allele Frequency (MAF) above the threshold (default: \(0.10\)), the engine “rescues” the candidate by introducing a degenerate IUPAC base (e.g., \(R\) for \(A/G\), \(Y\) for \(C/T\)).
Complexity Constraint: To prevent signal dilution, the total degeneracy (calculated as the product of the degenerate base multiplicities) is capped at a maximum multiplier (default: \(16\), e.g., a primer with two 2-fold degenerate bases has a complexity of \(2 \times 2 = 4\)).
Worst-Case Thermodynamic Evaluation: The engine invokes ViennaRNA (Lorenz et al. 2011) to model secondary structures (hairpins, homodimers, heterodimers) for every individual nucleotide combination represented by the degenerate primer. The thermodynamic score is determined by the worst-performing variant to ensure amplification stability across all target viral strains.

4.1. PrimerLab Thermodynamic Master Template (primerlab_template.yaml)
PrimerLab calculates DNA melting temperatures (\(T_m\)) using nearest-neighbor thermodynamic parameters and models secondary structures using ViennaRNA (Lorenz et al. 2011). Below are the key parameters defined in the template:









Parameter Path
Allowed Values

Float \(\ge 0.0\)

Monovalent salt concentration (Na+ / K+ in mM). Used for salt-correction of DNA melting temperature.


parameters.thermodynamics.salt_divalent
Float \(\ge 0.0\)

Divalent salt concentration (Mg2+ in mM). RAA specific. Isothermal amplification relies on high magnesium concentrations (~14 mM) to stabilize recombinase-DNA complexes.


parameters.thermodynamics.dntp_conc
Float \(\ge 0.0\)

Concentration of dNTPs (mM). Higher than standard PCR to fuel fast isothermal transcription.


parameters.thermodynamics.dna_conc
Float \(\ge 0.0\)

Total primer concentration (nM). RAA requires a highly crowded environment to drive recombinase-mediated strand invasion.


parameters.primer_size.opt

Optimal length of RAA primers. Isothermal recombinase binding requires long primers (\(30-35\) bp) to successfully invade double-stranded DNA templates.


parameters.probe.type
"exo", "taqman"

The chemistry type. "exo" designs TwistAmp Exo-style probes (\(46-52\) bp) with an internal abasic site (THF spacer) for Endonuclease IV cleavage.


qc.vienna_ranking_limit
Integer
50
The top 50 candidates from Primer3 are sent to ViennaRNA to calculate secondary structures (hairpins, homodimers, heterodimers) at the isothermal temperature of \(37^\circ\text{C}\).





4.2. How to Interpret PrimerLab Design Outputs
Module 08 outputs best_primers.json containing the physical profiles of the designed set:

Hairpin & Dimer \(\Delta G\): Represents the Gibbs free energy change of self-folding. Values closer to 0 (e.g. \(>-2.0\text{ kcal/mol}\)) are stable and safe. Values more negative than \(-5.0\text{ kcal/mol}\) indicate a high risk of primer-dimer formation, which will consume master-mix and cause false positives.
Degeneracy Multiplier: The number of unique primer sequences in the synthesized mix. A multiplier of 16 (e.g. 4 degenerate positions) means the active concentration of any single primer sequence is diluted to \(1/16\)-th. Keeping this below 16 ensures high diagnostic sensitivity.

6. Troubleshooting & Limitations

6.1. High-Degeneracy Failures (Exceeding Multiplier)

Problem: PrimerLab fails to return candidates, throwing warnings that the degeneracy complexity limit (\(16\)) was exceeded.
Cause: This happens in variable zones (such as UTRs or HA loops) where multiple minor variants exist at rates \(>10\%\).
Solution: Shift the design target to a conserved coding region (e.g. M1 segment), increase the maf_threshold to \(0.15\) (to ignore rarer variants), or increase the max_multiplier to \(32\) (noting that this may lower overall reaction sensitivity).

title: Module 10: In-silico PCR & RAA Validation
text:
Before biological wet-lab validation, designed primer and probe candidates must undergo virtual simulation to measure their diagnostic sensitivity. Module 10 executes the In-silico Validation Engine (scripts/m10_insilico_pcr.py) using SeqKit (Shen et al. 2016) to run high-throughput binding simulations against large GISAID and NCBI sequence databases.
This step calculates exact diagnostic coverage metrics broken down by subtype, collection year, and country to verify assay robustness against global and local viral diversity.

title: Module 10: In-silico PCR & RAA Validation
text:
1. Virtual Amplification and Binding Simulation
The validation engine runs simulated amplifications by matching designed primers and probes against target database sequences using sequence-matching parameters:
                            ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                            │    final_candidates.json (M09)  │
                            └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │

                               │  (SeqKit Amplicon Simulator) │
                               └─────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                               │  Target Database Sequences   │
                               │  (50k+ GISAID Fasta Genomes) │
                               └─────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                               │   Mismatch Tolerance Filter  │
                               │  (3' Zone vs. Internal Body) │
                               └─────────────┬────────────────┘
                                             │
                                             ▼
                    ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
                    ▼                                                 ▼
      ┌──────────────────────────┐                      ┌──────────────────────────┐
      │   Amplified Sequences    │                      │   Missed/Failed Strains  │
      │   (Simulated Positive)   │                      │   (Diagnostic Escape)    │
      └──────────────────────────┘                      └──────────────────────────┘

1.1. PCR Simulation (seqkit amplicon)
SeqKit’s amplicon command matches primer sequences against every target genome in the database, allowing up to a defined number of mismatches (default: \(3\) or \(4\) mismatches). It returns virtual amplicons for target genomes that match both primers within a designated length range (e.g. 100–300 bp).


1.2. RAA Isothermal Binding Rules
Because RAA operates at \(37^\circ\text{C}\) with a recombinase complex, it is thermodynamically tolerant of minor internal mismatches but highly sensitive to 3’ terminal defects. The engine implements strict, multi-zone mismatch criteria:

3’ Critical Zone: Evaluates the last 8 nucleotides of the 3’ end of both primers. It allows a maximum of 1 mismatch; any more than 1 mismatch in this zone vetoes the binding.
Internal Body: Allows a maximum of 4 mismatches across the rest of the 30–35 bp primer body.
Probe Binding: Probes (46–52 bp) allow a maximum of 3 mismatches to maintain hybridization-induced exonuclease cleavage.

title: Module 10: In-silico PCR & RAA Validation
text:
2. Spatial and Temporal Coverage Aggregation
To identify potential diagnostic gaps, the engine aggregates simulation results into distinct metadata dimensions:

Subtype Coverage: Breaks down detection percentages by viral sub-lineages (e.g., A/H1N1, A/H3N2, A/H5N1) to ensure the assay is truly universal.
Temporal Coverage: Groups detection rates by year of sequence collection (e.g., 2015 to 2025) to track whether modern evolutionary mutations are lowering assay sensitivity over time.
Spatial Coverage: Groups detection rates by country (e.g., Indonesia vs. global) to guarantee high local diagnostic sensitivity.

5. Troubleshooting & Limitations

5.1. Low RAA Coverage compared to PCR Coverage

Problem: The RAA amplified percentage is significantly lower than the PCR amplified percentage.
Cause: This occurs in target sets with high sequence variability. RAA primers are longer (30–35 bp) than PCR primers (20 bp), which statistically increases the probability of encountering mismatches along the primer body. In addition, the strict 3’ terminal zone limit (max 1 mismatch in 8 bp) penalizes binding much harder than standard PCR.
Solution: Turn on degenerate base rescue in Module 08 to introduce degenerate bases at variable sites, allowing the primer to match multiple variants and restore RAA coverage.

title: Results: Diagnostic Candidate Generation
text:
This section details the biophysical, thermodynamic, and specificity profiles of the primary and alternative diagnostic candidates generated by the pipeline.
By running three distinct geographical filtering scenarios, we track how database constraints shape the molecular properties, degeneracy, and safety of the resulting primer and probe sets:

title: Results: Diagnostic Candidate Generation

title: Results: Diagnostic Candidate Generation
text:
2. Secondary Structure Stability (Thermodynamic Safety)
To prevent self-priming, hairpin loops, and primer-dimer complexes, the engine evaluated each set’s free energy (\(\Delta G\)):

Hairpin Veto Threshold (\(\Delta G \le -9.0\) kcal/mol): Hairpins with strong folding energies can block polymerase extension. All M1 design candidates (Indo-only and SEA-only) showed a hairpin \(\Delta G\) of -4.21 kcal/mol, and M2 candidates (All-partial) showed -2.81 kcal/mol, which are well within the safe range (\(>-9.0\) kcal/mol).
Cross-Dimer Veto Threshold (\(\Delta G \le -12.0\) kcal/mol): Primer-dimers compete with target amplification. The cross-dimerization energies range from -7.59 to -9.30 kcal/mol, showing that stable primer dimers are thermodynamically unfavorable under standard PCR cycling conditions.

section: 3. IUPAC Degeneracy and Target Coverage Trade-offs
text:
3. IUPAC Degeneracy and Target Coverage Trade-offs
IUPAC degenerate bases (such as R for A/G, Y for C/T, K for G/T) are added to primer sequences to ensure the assay can bind to templates containing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) circulating in the population:

Regional Designs (Indo-Only & SEA-Only):

Designed in the conserved 187–352 bp M1 region, the primers require a degeneracy multiplier of 16 to achieve \(>99.5\%\) coverage of local sequences. This low degeneracy count is ideal because high degeneracy can dilute the concentration of the active primer species in the PCR mix.

Global Design (All-Partial):

Because global background sequences introduce high entropy, the M2 target primers require a degeneracy multiplier of 16 for Rank 1 and 2, but Rank 3 requires a higher degeneracy of 32 (on the forward primer) to accommodate global variation, illustrating how database size and geographic filters dictate degeneracy demands.

4. Specificity Verification and BLAST Veto Filtering
All generated candidates were filtered through the NCBI BLAST+ Specificity Verification Engine (Module 09) using local databases (human_db for host DNA and virus_db for non-target respiratory viruses).

3’ End Veto Filter Criteria
If a candidate pair matches any non-target respiratory pathogen or human sequence with zero mismatches in the last 8 nucleotides at the 3’ end, the set is vetoed (FAIL).

Indo-Only Vetoes: Out of 100 raw candidates, 12 sets were vetoed due to critical 3’ end cross-reactivity with the human genome (e.g. Candidate 5 and 18).
All-Partial Vetoes: 22 candidate sets were vetoed due to human genomic cross-reactivity.

title: Results: Phylodynamics & Evolutionary History
text:
To track how Influenza A Matrix Protein (MP) lineages have evolved and spread geographically, we executed maximum-likelihood phylogenetic reconstruction (IQ-TREE 2 (Minh et al. 2020)) and molecular clock modeling (TreeTime (Sagulenko et al. 2018)).
This section summarizes the database composition, quality filtering metrics, evolutionary rates, ancestral mutation paths, and spatio-temporal migration patterns of the MP segment.

title: Results: Phylodynamics & Evolutionary History
text:
1. Sequence Dataset Composition & Quality Control
To ensure high-fidelity evolutionary modeling, raw sequence libraries were subjected to strict quality control (QC) and deduplication filters:

Raw Sequence Database: The initial raw dataset compiled from GISAID and NCBI databases comprised 50,750 sequences covering the Influenza A MP segment.
Quality Filtering & Deduplication: High-standard sequence quality filtering (discarding sequences with \(> 5\%\) ambiguous N-content or invalid characters) followed by sequence deduplication of identical genomes resulted in 20,720 high-quality unique sequences.
Phylogenetic Subsampling: To run computational reconstruction while preserving evolutionary diversity, a balanced spatio-temporal subsampling strategy (grouped by clade, host, country, and collection year) was applied:

Indonesia Only Build: Selected 646 representative sequences (capturing H1N1, H3N2, and H5N1 subtypes collected in Indonesia).
Southeast Asia Only Build: Subsampled 2,000 representative sequences (from 2,681 available genomes).
All-Partial Database Build: Subsampled 2,000 representative sequences (from 6,629 available sequences in the all-partial database, comprising local Indonesian and global contextual strains).

Mutation Velocity (Substitution Rate):

The molecular clock model estimated the evolutionary rate of the MP segment to be \(3.00 \times 10^{-3}\) substitutions per site per year across all three datasets (as calculated by TreeTime (Sagulenko et al. 2018)). This estimate is consistent with published nucleotide substitution rates for human influenza A, where HA typically evolves at \(3\)–\(5 \times 10^{-3}\) substitutions per site per year (Bhatt et al. 2011), while the more structurally constrained Matrix segment exhibits lower rates in purely human seasonal lineages. The convergent rate across all three geographically diverse datasets confirms that the Matrix segment is a stable and temporally calibrated target for diagnostic design.

Temporal Root Estimation (TMRCA):

The most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) varies by dataset due to sampling scope:

Indonesia Only: Estimated around the year 1981.43 (indicating localized ancestral roots tracing to early 1980s).
Southeast Asia Only: Estimated around the year 1970.24.
All-Partial Database: Estimated around the year 1986.76.


Branch Lengths & Clades:

The tree topology exhibits distinct split patterns between the major sub-lineages, with H3N2 and H1N1 separating into deep, long-lived monophyletic branches, while H5N1 strains cluster into distinct geographic sub-clades.

title: Results: Phylodynamics & Evolutionary History
text:
3. Ancestral State Reconstruction & Mutation Mapping
Ancestral sequence reconstruction (using augur ancestral and augur translate) mapped the exact historical progression of nucleotide and amino acid substitutions across the phylogenetic tree:

M1 Protein Stability & High-Entropy Sites: The M1 matrix protein (which forms the structural scaffold beneath the viral envelope) is highly conserved overall, but contains specific highly variable residues. Diversity analysis identified several high-entropy positions—most notably at amino acid positions 15, 27, 30, 37, and 42 (with entropy \(\ge 0.6\)). These prominent peaks are primarily driven by subtype-specific differences between seasonal H1N1, H3N2, and avian H5N1. In contrast, the surrounding structural regions of M1 show complete conservation (diversity near \(0.0\)) across all lineages. This highlights why localized target scanning is critical to bypass these specific variable residues and focus on subtype-common anchors.
M2 Ion Channel Variation: In contrast, the M2 ion channel (involved in viral uncoating) showed localized clusters of mutations. Ancestral reconstruction successfully mapped the emergence and fixation of the S31N mutation (serine to asparagine at codon 31) in the M2 transmembrane domain. This substitution, which confers resistance to adamantane-class antivirals (amantadine and rimantadine), has been identified as a deep ancestral node event in H3N2 and H1N1pdm09 lineages (Hayden 2006; Deyde et al. 2007), and is now a near-universal feature of circulating seasonal Influenza A strains globally—including all Indonesian H3N2 and H1N1pdm09 sequences in this dataset.
Clade-Defining Mutational Signatures: Key amino acid substitutions (such as N82T and R210K in the M1 gene) were identified as clade-defining markers. By mapping these mutations to specific ancestral nodes, the pipeline validates that target regions chosen for primer design avoid these variable positions, preventing diagnostic mismatch against specific circulating sub-clades.

title: Results: Phylodynamics & Evolutionary History
text:
4. Subtype Divergence & Evolutionary Co-existence
The reconstructed tree topology highlights the deep evolutionary divergence between the three primary Influenza A subtypes circulating in Indonesia:

Seasonal H3N2: Represents a stable, long-term evolutionary lineage tracing back to the 1968 pandemic. The MP segment of H3N2 has accumulated mutations at a steady, clock-like rate, showing a clear linear relationship between collection year and root-to-tip distance.
H1N1pdm09: Displays a distinct evolutionary trajectory. The MP segment of this lineage originates from the Eurasian avian-like (EA) swine influenza lineage, as established by genomic analysis of the 2009 pandemic origin (Smith et al. 2009). The deep topological split between H1N1pdm09 and H3N2 in the phylogenetic tree confirms that these segments maintain separate genetic identity without inter-lineage recombination.
Avian H5N1: Clustered into highly distinct monophyletic branches separated from seasonal human influenza strains. The Indonesian H5N1 strains, primarily belonging to Clade 2.1.3 (Kandun et al. 2006), exhibit independent evolutionary rates reflecting their circulation in domestic poultry and wild bird reservoirs. This deep divergence—representing up to four decades of independent evolution—underscores why a single universal primer set must accommodate broad sequence variation to achieve adequate cross-subtype sensitivity.

title: Results: Phylodynamics & Evolutionary History
text:
5. Spatio-Temporal Dispersal Analysis (Nextstrain)
Using the metadata associated with the subsampled genomes (collection date and country), we mapped the historical migration pathways of the Matrix segment:

Indonesia as a Viral Reservoir:

Phylogeographic modeling shows frequent introduction events into Southeast Asia, with Indonesia acting as a stable sink and occasional source for avian-origin H5N1 clades.

Regional SEA Connectivity:

Strong regional transmission pathways are visible between Indonesia, Singapore, and Malaysia, particularly for seasonal H3N2 strains. This high connectivity explains why the sea-only design shares target similarities with the indo-only design but remains biased when evaluated globally.
